problem: VLN agents fine-tuned for one scene/illumination condition catastrophically forget others. LoRA and MoE-LoRA variants use 2D matrices (one shared factor plus task-specific ones), so they can only represent two knowledge levels and cannot decouple scene and environment knowledge.
motivation: Real deployment exposes agents to many scenes and illumination conditions (low-light, overexposure, scattering) in sequence, so they must learn continually without forgetting. Navigation knowledge is naturally hierarchical (core skills, scene, environment), which suggests a high-order tensor representation.
key_idea: Represent LoRA-style adaptation as a 4th-order tensor with Tucker decomposition (shared core, encoder and decoder plus scene and environment expert factor matrices), and learn it continually with EWC on shared parts and consistency and orthogonality constraints on experts.
insight: Decoupling scene and environment into separate expert factors within one tensor beats coupled or matrix-based hierarchies. A 3rd-order tensor with coupled scene-environment experts gives 54 SR versus 65 for 4th-order. A three-level hierarchical LoRA (ABC-LoRA) gives 55 SR, better than O-LoRA (51) but below TuKA. Sharing the core tensor and encoder matters; without sharing the core tensor SR drops from 65 to 53-55. Sharing the decoder mainly saves storage. Larger expert ranks help more than larger shared ranks, with saturation.
method: TuKA: the adapter weight is a 4th-order tensor a×b×M×N decomposed by Tucker into core G, decoder U1, encoder U2, scene experts U3 (M×r3) and environment experts U4 (N×r4). Per task, one row each of U3 and U4 is selected, giving ΔW = U1·(G×3 U3[s]×4 U4[e])·U2^T, which is a 2D matrix that aligns with LLM weights. Ranks are (8,8,64,64) with M=7 and N=4, about 0.3M params per adapted layer.

Inheritance of shared knowledge: G, U1 and U2 carry over across tasks, and a scene or environment expert is initialized from its earlier version if it was seen before. An EWC loss with Fisher information (EMA-updated with ω) protects the shared parts.

Expert-specific learning: experts of other scenes and environments are frozen, and only the current U3[s] and U4[e] are trained. A consistency loss keeps reused experts close to their old values, and a row-orthogonality loss makes new experts orthogonal to old ones.
Total loss: autoregressive action loss weighted by λ=1-(λ1+λ2+λ3), plus L_ewc, L_co and L_es with λ1=0.2, λ2=0.2, λ3=0.1.

Task-specific expert search: CLIP visual features per scene and per environment are stored during training. At test time, cosine similarity between current observation features and the stored sets picks the scene and environment experts, so task IDs are not needed.

Allday-Habitat platform: normal Habitat renderings are degraded with an atmospheric scattering model, a low-light noise/gamma model and an overexposure clip/saturation model. The benchmark has 24 sequential tasks: 5 sim scenes × 4 environments plus 2 real-world scenes × (normal, low-light).
AlldayWalker: StreamVLN (Qwen2-7B with CLIP vision encoder) equipped with TuKA and DKIL.

setting.backbone: StreamVLN (Qwen2-7B LLM + CLIP vision encoder) with TuKA adapters, fine-tuned sequentially
setting.model_size: 7B base; ~0.3M TuKA params per adapted layer; 15.64M trainable params total
setting.training_data: About 400-460 training episodes per task over 24 sequential tasks (20 simulated Habitat/MP3D scenes×degradations plus 4 real-world captured scenes); 10 epochs per task
setting.observation: monocular RGB video stream (history frames) plus language instruction
setting.action_space: low-level FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN LEFT 15° / TURN RIGHT 15° / STOP
setting.simulator: Habitat (extended Allday-Habitat with degradation models) plus real-world scenes
setting.privileged: none at test time (task ID is hidden, experts chosen by CLIP retrieval; training uses task IDs)

numbers.extra: Sequential training on 24 tasks; task ID unknown at test time (CLIP expert retrieval); ~100-150 test episodes per task; 8 GPUs. Averages over 24 tasks for SR/F-SR.

numbers_note: Per-task tables exist; only averages are recorded here. Not R2R/RxR-style benchmarks; a custom benchmark was created. No standard NE or TL reported.
results: AlldayWalker reaches an average SR of 65% with F-SR 11 over 24 tasks, versus SD-LoRA at 56 (F-SR 18) and O-LoRA at 52, using comparable trainable parameters. Test-time adaptation baselines FSTTA (44) and FeedTTA (50) are lower. On unseen scenarios it obtains 55 SR versus 39-40 for SD-LoRA and BranchLoRA.
limitations: Evaluated only on a self-constructed benchmark with synthetic degradations, 100-150 test episodes per task, and limited real-world scenes; no standard VLN benchmarks (R2R-CE, RxR-CE).

Expert selection depends on CLIP feature retrieval and stored features per scene and environment, and the number of experts M and N must be set in advance; new scenes/environments beyond the pre-set expert count are not addressed.
SPL/OSR not reported for real-world tasks, and average SR is still low on some hard tasks (e.g., T2 at 23, T5 at 33).
